faq.q: What do you write on a QR code sign for wedding photos?
faq.a: Write a short headline with one verb (“Scan to share your photos”), one instruction line (“Open your phone camera and point it here”), and one line about what happens next, such as when the album opens. Add a backup link or join code in small type. Leave off long URLs, logos and extra hashtags so the one action stands out.

faq.q: How big should a QR code be on a wedding table sign?
faq.a: About 2 to 3 inches wide on a 5 × 7 inch table card. The common rule is to make the code one tenth as wide as the scanning distance, then add 20 to 30% for dim light, so a guest sitting 2 feet away needs a code about 3 inches wide. Welcome signs read from 3 to 5 feet away need codes about 4.5 to 7.5 inches wide.

faq.q: Can Android guests scan a wedding QR code?
faq.a: Yes. Most Android phones read QR codes from the built-in camera app or Google Lens, and iPhones read them from the Camera app. What matters more is where the code leads. Test that the page opens in a normal browser on both kinds of phone, without a login wall or an app that only works on one platform.

faq.q: Should the photo sign also show our wedding hashtag?
faq.a: You can, but keep it secondary. One clear action is easier to follow than two competing ones. Hashtags only gather public posts, so put the QR code first and give the hashtag a small line underneath, or its own sign near the photo booth.

faq.q: What if the QR code doesn’t scan on the day?
faq.a: Print a short link or join code under every code so guests can type it. Ask one friend to be the go-to person for anyone who gets stuck, and keep the link in your phone so it can be texted on the spot. Small, glossy or low-contrast codes are the usual culprits, and a proof print catches all three.
